title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 7 (03/12/2018)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 3 DECEMBER 2018
Subject: The Claimant challenged one of the Arbitrators (appointed by the Respondent)
pursuant to Article 11 of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules 1976.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of Redacted to preserve anonymity
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the Arbitrator’s prior and parallel appointments in
other cases, and instructions by other members of the Arbitrator’s chambers.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
As London was the seat of arbitration, English law, as the curial law, was
relevant.
The test for apparent bias under English law and the IBA Conflicts Guidelines
is an objective one and is not dependent on the particular characteristics of
the parties.
The fair-minded observer under English law is assumed to be informed of the
relevant circumstances, including how the legal profession operates (and
particularly, as relevant here, the English Bar’s “chambers system”).
The Arbitrator’s prior appointment in a case involving the appointing Party in
this case, which concluded seven years ago, does not, objectively, give rise to
concerns regarding the appearance of bias after that length of time. This
conclusion is reinforced by the fact that: (i) in the previous case the Arbitrator
acted as sole arbitrator (jointly appointed by the parties) rather than as an
appointee of the current appointing Party and (ii) in that case the Arbitrator
found against that Party.
The Arbitrator’s appointment as presiding arbitrator in an active case involving
the Respondent’s parent entity (which is equated with the Respondent for the
purposes of the challenge) does not, objectively, raise justifiable doubts as to
the Arbitrator’s impartiality or independence. The answer would be the same
even if the Arbitrator had been a party-appointee (as opposed to a presiding
arbitrator) in the prior case. The fact of a single prior appointment by a party,
even in an ongoing arbitration (of which the outcome will not yet be known),
would not, in and of itself, raise justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s
impartiality or independence.

The Arbitrator’s prior appointment in another case by an unconnected party
represented by the same law firm that represents the Respondent in this
arbitration does not give rise to justifiable doubts regarding the Arbitrator’s
impartiality or independence, even if considered cumulatively with the other
appointments mentioned.
A failure to explain the practical arrangements for ensuring information
barriers between members of the Arbitrator’s chambers cannot be seen as
calling into question the Arbitrator’s impartiality.
No justifiable doubts regarding the impartiality or independence of the
Arbitrator arise solely on the basis of instructions received, or to be received,
from a particular party on other matters by other members of the Arbitrator's
chambers, particularly where the contribution to the overall chambers'
workload of such instructions is extremely limited.
A delay of 15 days from the Arbitrator’s nomination to make a disclosure does
not raise justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s impartiality or independence,
in circumstances where the disclosure was made prior to the constitution of
the Tribunal and before any substantive steps were taken in the arbitration,
which was a “short and inconsequential” delay in the circumstances and, in
any event, there was not a clear obligation to make a disclosure.
No justifiable doubts as to impartiality or independence arose where the
Arbitrator declined to answer certain questions posed by the challenging Party
on the basis that: (i) the Arbitrator had already disclosed relevant matters; and
(ii) the questions related to the internal business practices of the Arbitrator’s
chambers or its members. If the Arbitrator felt that there were no further
disclosures to be made, or that the Arbitrator was being asked for information
too inappropriate to be given, it was reasonable for the Arbitrator to say so.

Decision 7 - 4

Introduction
1. This is the decision […] of the LCIA Court on a challenge that has been brought by the Claimant […]
against [A]. [A] was appointed as arbitrator by the Respondent […] in proceedings between the
Claimant and the Respondent (together the “Parties”) commenced by a Notice of Arbitration dated
21 August 2018 (the “Arbitration”).
2. Following this introduction I shall provide details of the Arbitration and the background to the
challenge against [A]. I shall then describe the basis for the challenge and address the position of
[Government B], before turning to the criteria to be applied in determining the challenge. I shall then
address the facts said to give rise to the challenge, both individually and cumulatively, by reference to
the criteria identified. My decision on the challenge is set out in paragraph 122 below.
The Arbitration
3. The Arbitration concerns a dispute arising out of a[n] […] Agreement […] dated 4 November 2003, as
amended, between the Parties and a related Letter of Intent dated 13 September 2017 agreed
between the Parties and [Government B]. The Claimant maintains that the Respondent has breached
the terms of the [Agreement] and the Letter of Intent and unlawfully imposed a restriction on the
power going to the Claimant’s mine in [Country B] as a means of coercing the Claimant to pay higher
electricity tariffs.1
4. The Parties’ arbitration agreement is set out in clauses 23 and 24 of the [Agreement], as amended,
which provide as follows:
“23. Disputes
If any dispute arises relating to this Agreement or any claims for damages is made as the result of
breach of any obligation hereunder (including, but not limited to, any claims for damages arising under
paragraph 20), the parties shall use their best efforts to resolve such disputes through good faith
negotiation. Each party shall designate executive management and/or other senior representatives to
conduct such good faith negotiations. Any dispute or claim for, as applicable, not resolved by such
negotiation, within 21 days of one party notifying the other of the existence of the dispute shall be
resolved by arbitration as provided in paragraph 24 of this Agreement by the service of either party of
the notice of intention to arbitrate referred to in paragraph 24(a). While a dispute is continuing, both
[the Claimant] and [the Respondent] are required to continue to perform their respective obligations
under this Agreement (including, without limitation with respect to each of the parties, in the case of
[the Claimant], the making of any payment due to [the Respondent] and, in the case of [the
Respondent] the tendering of electrical power to the [Claimant], other than, with respect to [the
Respondent]’s obligation to tender electrical power, in circumstances specified in paragraph 5(b)
and/or paragraphs 13 and 21 and, with respect to [the Claimant]’s obligations to make payments [the
Respondent], in circumstances specified in paragraph 14, and/or paragraphs 15(e), until such dispute
has been fully and finally resolved).
24. Arbitration Procedures
1 There is no provision for a response or answer to the Notice of Arbitration under the applicable rules, but
the Parties have proceeded with constituting the Tribunal to determine the Claimant’s claims.
Decision 7 - 5

(a) Either party can initiate arbitration by notice of intention to arbitrate to the other party stating the
dispute or claim for damages, as applicable, to be arbitrated. Upon the giving of such notice the dispute
or claim for damages, as applicable, shall be determined by an arbitrator who is agreed upon in writing
by the parties. Failing such agreement within four weeks after notice by either party, the arbitrator
shall be appointed upon the application of either party to the President of the London International
Court of Arbitration. The tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator. Any arbitration shall be conducted
under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules subject to modifications as the parties may agree in writing (“the
Rules“). The arbitrator shall be a person whose profession and experience make him qualified to
consider the dispute.
(b) Any arbitration shall be held at [S], [Country B] or, at the request of either party, at such other place
as may be agreed upon by those involved in arbitration and failing such agreement in London England.
(c) The arbitration proceedings shall be conducted in the English language. The decision of the
arbitrator shall be given in writing as soon as reasonably possible.
(d) An award in proceedings under the Rules shall be binding on the parties and judgement thereon
may be entered in any court having jurisdiction for the purpose.
(e) Unless otherwise agreed or provided, the cost of any arbitration procedure will be borne by the
unsuccessful party in accordance with the Rules.
(f) Where a dispute has been referred for settlement by arbitration in accordance with the Rules then
neither party shall be entitled to exercise any rights or election arising in consequence of any alleged
default by the other arising out of the subject matter of the dispute until the dispute has been resolved
by the decision of the arbitrator.
(g) All proceedings held by the parties for the purpose of resolving disputes shall be held in private and
except as permitted or required by under any other provision of this Agreement, shall not be open to
third parties.”
5. The Parties agreed, in an exchange of letters dated 10 and 26 July 2018 respectively between their
counsel, [C] on behalf of the Claimant and [D] on behalf of the Respondent, to vary the arbitration
agreement. They agreed to amend the requirement for a sole arbitrator to provide for a three-
member panel, with one arbitrator to be nominated by each party and a chair appointed by those
nominees.
6. Pursuant to clause 32 of the [Agreement] it is to be governed and construed in accordance with the
laws of [Country B]. Nothing in relation to the challenge to [A] is said to turn on [Country B’s] law, and
neither party has sought to make submissions on it.
Background to the Challenge
7. As mentioned in paragraph 1 above, the Arbitration was commenced by a Notice of Arbitration dated
21 August 2018, in which the Claimant nominated [E] as arbitrator.
8. The Arbitration was commenced under the Arbitration Rules of the United Nations Commission on
International Trade Law 1976 (the “1976 UNCITRAL Rules”), although the Claimant noted that the
tribunal will be invited to give its views on whether the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules or some later version of
Decision 7 - 6

them is to be applied. Pursuant to Article 7.1 of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules, each party shall “appoint”
one arbitrator and accordingly the nomination of arbitrators by the Parties falls to be treated as the
appointment of them under the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules.
9. In its Notice of Arbitration the Claimant states that the seat of the arbitration is London, England, by
agreement of the parties or because it is the default seat under paragraph 24(b) of the [Agreement].
10. On 4 September 2018 [D] wrote to [C] confirming that they were instructed to act for the Respondent
in the Arbitration and indicating that the Respondent intended to appoint [A] as arbitrator. [D] also
confirmed that [A] had indicated that if nominated he would require it to be disclosed that in the last
10 years “(a) he has acted as sole arbitrator in an arbitration (completed in 2011) to which [the
Respondent] was a party and (b) that he has received one appointment as a party appointed arbitrator
from a party represented by [D] (arbitration completed in 2014).” [D] requested confirmation whether
any objection would be made to [A]'s nomination on the basis of the matters disclosed. [D] further
noted its belief that [A] is independent and impartial but wished “to give you the opportunity to
comment at this stage to avoid potential delay later.”
11. By letter dated 6 September 2018, [C] responded to [D] that it would object to [A]’s appointment as
arbitrator on the basis that what had been disclosed “casts clear doubts over his impartiality and
suitability for this arbitration.” [C] also stated it was aware that [A]’s Chambers […] has several
barristers who currently act for the [Government B] and/or its related parastatals in arbitrations as
well as English court proceedings. This was said to raise an additional concern about the practical
management of ethical barriers2 with those other proceedings.
12. The Claimant does not anywhere specifically explain what precisely it means by references to an
“ethical barrier” or “ethical wall”. In this context it is reasonable to assume that it is intended to refer
to arrangements that would preclude [A] and other members of [X Chambers] sharing any information
regarding either the Arbitration or those matters involving [Country B] on which other members of [X
Chambers] are working. These terms will therefore be treated as referring to an information barrier
or, as it is sometimes called, a ‘Chinese Wall’.
13. By letter dated 7 September 2018 [D], indicated to [C] that it had passed the comments in [C]’s letter
of 6 September 2018 to [A] for his observations. [D] also noted it did not accept any of the matters
disclosed as being grounds for objection under the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in
International Arbitration (the “IBA Guidelines”),3 particularly given that as sole arbitrator [A] had
found against the Respondent.
14. By letter dated 12 September 2018 from [D] to [C], the Respondent nominated [A] as arbitrator. [D]
stated it had referred [C]’s comments to [A] who “has confirmed that he has no conflict of interest in
being appointed as [the Respondent]’s party appointed arbitrator.”
15. By letter dated 17 September 2018 (the “17 September letter”), [C] wrote again to [D] confirming that
it had pursued further enquiries about [A]’s work concerning [Government B] and its affiliates (which
2 The letter in fact refers to “ethical barristers” but I assume this to be a typographical error.
3 The letter refers simply to the “IBA guidelines” but it seems clear from subsequent correspondence that
this was a reference to the International Bar Associations’ 2010 Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest in
International Arbitration.
Decision 7 - 7

it said included the [Respondent]), including work by members of [X Chambers]. Those enquiries were
said to demonstrate that “many other [X Chambers’] members enjoy a long-standing and thriving
practice on instructions from [Government B], in many cases against [the Claimant]”. [C] also raised
concern that these matters were not proactively disclosed and suggested that the concerns it had
raised over [X Chambers’] management of ethical walls had gone “entirely ignored”. The letter went
on to set out “some information in the public domain” regarding work done by certain named
members of [X Chambers] (the “relevant [Chambers’] Members”) in relation to [Country B] but it also
included information known to [C] as a result of its representation of [the Claimant] in an UNCITRAL
arbitration. This information is discussed further below.
16. In the 17 September letter [C] also referred to the IBA Guidelines, and in particular General Standard
3 and paragraph 3.3.2 of the Orange List, and stated that the Claimant requested full disclosure, as
soon as possible, by [A]/[the Respondent]/[D] in relation to 14 questions set out in the letter.
17. By letter dated 27 September 2018, [D] responded to [C], again confirming [A]’s view that he
considered himself to be impartial and independent of the parties and stating that the Respondent
intended that he should remain in place. [D] commented that although the Claimant’s rights had been
reserved it had not specifically objected to [A]’s appointment. In addition [D] provided responses to
[C]’s 14 questions4 including the disclosure that [A] was acting as chair in an arbitration to which the
[Government B] is a party.
18. By letter dated 3 October 2018, [C] stated that they had validly objected and continue to object to
[A]’s appointment. The letter repeated a number of the concerns previously raised and stated that
they were “unimpressed by the lack of willingness to explain the practical management of ethical
walls” at [X Chambers] given the volume and frequency of instructions including current matters
adverse to the Claimant. They further indicated that the Claimant would take its objection to [A]’s
nomination to the LCIA and set out certain proposals for doing so.
19. [D] and [C] exchanged a number of further letters regarding, among other things, whether the
challenge had been notified within the time limit provided in the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules. These
exchanges resulted in agreement between the parties that the contested matter of [A]’s nomination
by the Respondent should be presented to the LCIA.
20. By letter dated 10 October 2018 to the LCIA, signed by both [D] and [C] and copied to the two
appointed arbitrators, the Parties confirmed that they agreed the challenge to [A]’s appointment (and
the fact of whether it had been made in time) should be referred to the LCIA for determination. By
email dated 17 October 2018 the LCIA confirmed that the LCIA Court was content to decide the matter
in accordance with the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules.5
21. Pursuant to clause 24(a) of the [Agreement], the designated appointing authority is “the President of
the London International Court of Arbitration”. Article 12(b) of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules provides that
if a challenge is not agreed and the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw, the decision on the
4 [D]’s letter refers to “13 questions” but in fact responded to all 14 questions posed.
5 The LCIA’s email refers to Article 13 of the UNCITRAL Rules. This should in fact be a reference to Article
12 of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules, which is the equivalent provision to Article 13 in the current version of
the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules.
Decision 7 - 8

challenge will be made by the designated appointing authority, at least when that appointing authority
did not make the initial appointment.
22. By letter dated 23 October 2018 addressed to me […], the Claimant made its application “for the
disqualification and/or removal and/or non-confirmation” of [A] as an arbitrator in the Arbitration (the
“Challenge”).
23. By letter dated 30 October 2018 the LCIA notified the Parties, copied to the two appointed arbitrators
and to me, that pursuant to Articles D.1(b) and D.3(a) of the Constitution of the LCIA Court, the LCIA
Court had appointed me […] to determine the Challenge.
24. The Respondent filed submissions in response to the Challenge on 1 November 2018 (the “Response”)
requesting the LCIA Court to reject the Challenge.
25. [A] has not recused himself.
The Basis of the Challenge
26. The Challenge is brought on what the Claimant describes in paragraph 44 of the Challenge as three
“key” grounds, namely (1) the conflict of interest and/or lack of independence and/or apparent bias
of [A], and/or (2) the breach of the duty of disclosure, and/or (3) the “intransigent stance on disclosure
of other relevant circumstances that justify [the Claimant’s] concerns”.
27. The Respondent says that it understands the Challenge to be brought on the basis of “conflicts of
interest and apparent bias” rather than a suggestion of actual bias on the part of [A]. This accords with
my understanding based on the Challenge and in particular paragraph 62 which refers to “justifiable
doubts as to [A]’s impartiality and/or independence”.
28. There was a dispute in the correspondence between [C] and [D] about whether the Claimant’s
objection to [A] was raised in time. Article 11.1 of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules provides that a party who
intends to challenge an arbitrator shall send notice of the challenge within fifteen days after being
notified of the appointment of the challenged arbitrator or within fifteen days after the circumstances
giving rise to the challenge become known to that party. However, whilst maintaining its position that
the time limit was not complied with, the Respondent stated in the Response that it had concluded it
would be preferable for the outcome of the Challenge to be based on the substantive allegations. The
Respondent confirmed it did not rely on an argument that the Challenge was out of time and was
content for the LCIA Court to proceed on the basis that it was timely.
29. The Claimant challenges [A] on the basis that the following alleged facts and circumstances are said
to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality and/or independence:
(a) [A]’s prior appointments as an arbitrator in cases involving the Respondent, [D] and
[Government B]; and
(b) [A]’s “late” disclosure of his appointment as an arbitrator in a case currently being conducted
in which [Government B] is a party and its dismissal as being “irrelevant”; and
(c) The instruction, including by [Government B], of the relevant [X Chambers’] Members in a
“high volume of substantial, highly valuable and politically significant instructions”, which
Decision 7 - 9

include many cases against [the Claimant]; and
(d) [A] having “drip-fed” information and failed to answer queries posed on behalf of the
Claimant.
30. As regards (c) above, the precise nature of the challenge being made is not entirely clear. Paragraph
44 of the Challenge, which sets out what are described as the “key grounds” for the Claimant’s
objection, does not refer at all to the relevant [X Chambers’] Members. It refers to “the intransigent
stance on disclosure of other relevant circumstances that justify [the Claimant’s] concern”, but this
seems more in keeping with (d) above. In correspondence from [C] to [D], and in particular the letters
dated 6 and 12 September 2018, the Claimant complains about a lack of proactive disclosure and that
concerns over [X Chambers’] management of ethical walls had not been addressed. However
elsewhere the nature of the objection appears to be more far-reaching. In particular in paragraph 40
of the Challenge it is said that “[A]’s resistance to address how [X Chambers] manages these various
instructions raises clear and justifiable concerns about this overwhelming concentration of repeat
instructions for a certain government by a single London-based chambers.” This appears to suggest
that the volume of instructions is also a concern. I shall therefore treat (c) as relating to both an alleged
lack of information being provided by [A] regarding any ethical walls, and also as one based on the
volume of instructions [X Chambers] receives from the Respondent or [Government B].
31. For the avoidance of doubt, I do not understand the Claimant to be saying that [A]’s disclosure
obligations entail a requirement that he disclose details of appointments or instructions received by
the other members of [X Chambers]. The Respondent has sought to address this proposition in the
Response, but paragraph 44 of the Challenge makes clear that the alleged breach of the duty of
disclosure relates in particular to the alleged late disclosure and the suggestion it was irrelevant.6
32. The Claimant makes clear it considers that the matters upon which it relies should be considered
cumulatively in determining whether justifiable doubts exist as to [A]’s impartiality and/or
independence. I accept that this is the correct approach.
33. In response the Respondent maintains that the Challenge should be rejected on the basis that:
(a) [A], an experienced international arbitrator, has confirmed that he considers himself to be impartial
and independent of the parties.
(b) [A] has not failed to disclose any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his
impartiality or independence.
(c) The instruction by [Government B] of the relevant [X Chambers’] Members in relation to matters
unconnected with the present arbitration was not and is not disclosable by [A] and he and the
Respondent were entitled not to provide answers to certain questions relating to those matters and
other matters concerning [X Chambers’] internal administration.
6 Similarly paragraph 65 of the Challenge makes clear that the concerns regarding alleged lack of disclosure
are that there was late disclosure. As regards disclosure of instructions received by other members of
chambers generally, see paragraph 90 below.
Decision 7 - 10

(d) Overall, the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the matters relied on by the
Claimant, would not conclude that there was a real possibility that [A] was biased.
Criteria to be applied
34. As mentioned in paragraph 8, the arbitration was commenced under the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules and I
find that the Challenge falls to be determined under those rules.
35. The challenge of arbitrators is dealt with under Articles 9 to 12 of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules which
provide in relevant part as follows:
“Article 9
A prospective arbitrator shall disclose to those who approach him in connexion with his possible
appointment any circumstances likely to give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or
independence. An arbitrator, once appointed or chosen, shall disclose such circumstances to the parties
unless they have already been informed by him of these circumstances.
Article 10
1. Any arbitrator may be challenged if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
arbitrators impartiality or independence…
Article 11
1. A party who intends to challenge an arbitrator shall send notice of his challenge within fifteen days
after the appointment of the challenged arbitrator has been notified to the challenging party or within
fifteen days after the circumstances mentioned in articles 9 and 10 became known to that party.
2. The challenge shall be notified to the other party, to the arbitrator who is challenged and to the
other members of the arbitral tribunal. The notification shall be in writing and shall state the reasons
for the challenge.
3. When an arbitrator has been challenged by one party, the other party may agree to the challenge.
The arbitrator may also, after the challenge, withdraw from his office. In neither case does this imply
acceptance of the validity of the grounds for the challenge.
Article 12
1. If the other party does not agree to the challenge and the challenged arbitrator does not withdraw,
the decision on the challenge will be made:
…
(b) When the initial appointment was not made by an appointing authority, but an appointing
authority has been previously designated, by that authority…”
36. It is common ground that London is the seat of the Arbitration. In those circumstances, English law, as
the curial law, is also relevant. The Parties have relied extensively on citations of English law in the
Challenge and the Response.
37. Pursuant to section 24(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, an arbitrator may be removed on the grounds
‘that circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality.’ The test for
impartiality under English law is “whether the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered
Decision 7 - 11

the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased”.7 Under English
law the “fair-minded and informed observer” is assumed to adopt a balanced approach and is neither
complacent nor unduly sensitive or suspicious.8 The test is objective and all factors that are said to
give rise to the possibility of apparent bias must be considered cumulatively.9
38. Both Parties have also referred extensively to the IBA Guidelines, both in their correspondence with
each other and in their submissions to me. In light of this I consider it appropriate for me to take
guidance from the IBA Guidelines, particularly as regards the specific circumstances relied upon for
the Challenge. I do so albeit recognising that they are not formally binding on me or on the Parties.
39. Under the heading “Conflicts of Interest”, General Standard 2 of the IBA Guidelines provides:
“(a) An arbitrator shall decline to accept an appointment or, if the arbitration has already been
commenced, refuse to continue to act as an arbitrator, if he or she has any doubt as to his or her ability
to be impartial or independent.
(b) The same principle applies if facts or circumstances exist, or have arisen since the appointment, which,
from the point of view of a reasonable third person having knowledge of the relevant facts and
circumstances, would give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence...
(c) Doubts are justifiable if a reasonable third person, having knowledge of the relevant facts and
circumstances, would reach the conclusion that there is a likelihood that the arbitrator may be
influenced by factors other than the merits of the case as presented by the parties in reaching his or
her decision.”
40. Accordingly an arbitrator may be challenged if there are justifiable doubts as to his or her impartiality
or independence. Whether there are such justifiable doubts has to be assessed by reference to how
they would be viewed by a fair-minded third party knowledgeable of the relevant facts and
circumstances.
The Parties’ Specific Characteristics
41. The Claimant has described itself as a party “foreign to the workings of the English chambers system”
and argues that “when considering the nature of barristers’ chambers, it is important to bear in mind
that this unique business structure may be particularly disquieting to parties like [the Claimant] which
are not familiar with the workings of the English bar.” This is against the background that the Claimant
describes itself as “[an entity from Country B] sitting within a [group from F], where the legal direction
of the arbitration is given from [Country G].” It is perhaps curious that those providing legal direction
from [Country G] would consider the English chambers system foreign, given its similarities to that
adopted in [Country G].
42. The Claimant also relies upon Hrvastska Elektroprivreda v The Republic of Slovenia (ICSID Case No.
ARB/05/24) (“Slovenia”) as support for its argument that the unfamiliarity of a party with the London
7 Porter v Magill [2001] UKHL 67 at [103] per Lord Hope.
8 Lawal v Northern Spirit [2004] 1 All ER 187, at [14] (Lord Steyn).
9 Cofely Limited v. Anthony Bingham [2016] EWHC 240 (Comm) para. 115.
Decision 7 - 12

chambers system is one of the circumstances to be taken into consideration in a challenge for
apparent bias, which must be looked at from the perspective of the specific parties.
43. The Respondent rejects the suggestion that whether or not there is apparent bias can depend upon
the personal characteristics of a party, such as nationality, on the basis that does not reflect the
position under English law. The Respondent also points out at paragraph 6.2 of the Response that the
Claimant’s own arbitrator, [E], is a member of the same chambers as counsel who represented the
Claimant in an arbitration that concluded in 2016 and which related to matters potentially relevant to
the Arbitration. The Respondent does not suggest that there is anything improper in this or that
disclosure was required of it, but notes its assumption that the Claimant must have satisfied itself of
the propriety of [E’s] appointment.
44. I find that the test of apparent bias is an objective one, and explicitly so under both English law10 and
the IBA Guidelines, which refer to the point of view of a fair-minded and informed observer and a
reasonable third person respectively. Beyond those described in paragraph 37 above, the English
courts have not considered it necessary to delve into the characteristics to be attributed to the fair-
minded and informed observer who is regarded simply as a reasonable member of the public.11 In
these circumstances I find that the test of apparent bias is not dependent on the particular
characteristics of the parties but on a reasonable third-party observer. Moreover as a matter of English
law the fair-minded observer is assumed to be informed of the relevant circumstances, including how
the legal profession operates.12
45. It is true that the question of disclosure in international arbitration may involve a subjective element,
in that, for example, under General Standard 3 of the IBA Guidelines the test for disclosure is where
“facts or circumstances exist that may, in the eyes of the parties, give rise to doubts as to the
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence” (emphasis added). That subjective element is not, however,
contemplated by the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules and in any event relates to disclosure rather than a finding
of apparent bias.
The Role of [Government B]
46. The Claimant says that the Respondent is a “parastatal” of [Government B] as contemplated by the
commentary to Article 5 of the International Law Commission’s Draft Articles on Responsibility of
States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (2001). The Claimant concludes that “on any view,
[Government B] is an affiliate and the Respondent is an extension of the arm of [Government B].” It is
not disputed by the Respondent that [Government B] is indirectly the sole shareholder of the
Respondent and appoints its Board. The Claimant maintains that “the actions and decisions of the
[Government B] are expected to be material and highly relevant for this arbitration.” For its part the
10 See paragraph 37 above.
11 See for example Johnson v Johnson (2000) 201 CLR 488 at [53] per Kirby J, cited by Lord Steyn in Lawal v
Northern Spirit [ibid].
12 Cofely Ltd v Bingham [2016] 2 All ER (Comm), at [72] per Hamblen J: “Such a fair minded and informed

50. [A] has disclosed three prior appointments. In the first of these he was appointed as sole arbitrator in
a case involving the Respondent as a party (“Case One”). Case One concluded in 2011, some 7 years

agreement between their solicitors). Further the Respondent maintains that the award in Case One
was made after a fully contested hearing and included a finding against the Respondent on liability
and an award for the payment of “very substantial” damages by the Respondent to the other party.

appointing him was represented by [D], the law firm representing the Respondent in the Arbitration
(“Case Two”). Case Two concluded in 2014. The parties to it were unrelated to either of the Parties.
52. The third case disclosed by [A] concerns his appointment as chair of an ongoing arbitration in which
[Government B] is a party (“Case Three”).
53. Prior appointments in cases involving the appointing party can in principle give rise to concerns
regarding impartiality. The fact that an arbitrator receives frequent repeat appointments and derives
a high proportion of his or her income from arbitrations in which a particular party participates can be
relevant to a finding of bias.13 This might be the case for example if those appointments reach a level
where justifiable doubts might arise that the arbitrator’s decision-making may be influenced by factors
other than the merits of the case.
54. As regards prior appointments by a party, guidance is provided by paragraph 3.1.3 of Part II of the IBA
Guidelines which includes in its Orange List that: “The arbitrator has, within the past three years, been
13 Cofely Limited v. Anthony Bingham [2016] EWHC 240 (Comm) [103]-[115] (Hamblen J).

appointed as arbitrator on two or more occasions by one of the parties, or an affiliate of one of the
parties.”
55. Similarly, as regards the question of prior appointments by counsel, guidance is provided by paragraph
3.3.8 of Part II of the IBA Guidelines which includes in its Orange List the situation where: “The
arbitrator has, within the past three years, been appointed on more than three occasions by the same
counsel, or the same law firm.”
56. It is suggested by the Claimant in its submissions that both Case One and Case Two give rise to a
perception of bias and that this conclusion is supported by the fact that [A] felt compelled to make
the initial disclosure. If it is intended by this to suggest that the mere fact of there being matters which
ought properly to be disclosed gives rise to an appearance of bias, I reject that submission. As is clear
from General Standard 3(c) of the IBA Guidelines and the explanatory notes to it, “a disclosure does
not imply that the disclosed facts are such as to disqualify the arbitrator” on the basis of a conflict of
interest. This is similarly emphasised in paragraph 4 of Part II of the IBA Guidelines which makes clear
disclosure does not give rise to a presumption regarding disqualification. Indeed if at the outset of a
case the arbitrator considered there to be a conflict of interest he or she would decline the
appointment rather than making the disclosure in accordance with General Standard 2(a).
57. The purpose of disclosure is so that the parties can be fully informed of any facts or circumstances
that may be relevant and which they may wish to explore further. Under the IBA Guidelines any doubt
as to whether an arbitrator should disclose certain facts or circumstances should be resolved in favour
of disclosure.
58. It is, however, a separate question whether the matters disclosed give rise to a conflict of interest.
That will depend upon whether, viewed objectively by a third party with knowledge of the facts and
circumstances, they give rise to justifiable doubts concerning the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence.
59. [A]’s only appointment in a case specifically involving the Respondent was in Case One which
concluded 7 years ago. His further appointment by the Respondent in the Arbitration, after that length
of time, does not, objectively, give rise to concerns regarding the appearance of bias. Moreover, [D]
maintains not only that he was a sole arbitrator rather than an appointee of the Respondent, but that
he also found against the Respondent in Case One. These circumstances reinforce the conclusion that
[A]’s appointment in Case One does not, objectively, raise justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or
independence.
60. As mentioned above, I consider that for the purposes of determining the Challenge [Government B] is
to be equated with the Respondent. Accordingly [A]’s appointment in Case Three must also be
considered. He is the chair of that tribunal and it is not therefore a case in which he has been appointed
as arbitrator by [Government B]. Even if he had been so appointed, I find that the fact of a single prior
appointment by a party, even in an ongoing arbitration (of which the outcome will not yet be known),
would not, viewed objectively, raise justifiable doubts in and of itself as to his impartiality or
independence. Moreover even when viewed cumulatively with his appointment in Case One, I reject
the suggestion that these appointments are of a nature or frequency to give rise to justifiable doubts
regarding his impartiality or independence.

cumulatively with the other appointments referred to above.

depending on the circumstances, objectively concerns might arise that the arbitrator’s decision

rise to an appearance of bias, either on its own or when considered in combination with [A]’s
appointments in Case One and Case Three.

87. English barristers are self-employed practitioners for whom chambers have traditionally been viewed
as a means of organising the delivery of related administrative services. The development of chambers
in modern times has exposed that position to greater scrutiny, particularly in the context of
international arbitration. Collective marketing, including chambers branding and promotion, the costs
of which are shared by its members, have been viewed in some quarters as raising questions about
whether members of chambers are assuming a collective identity similar to a law firm.
88. Against that it remains the case that there are fundamental differences between law firms and
chambers. These include the fact that the members of chambers do not pool their earnings. Members
of chambers are remunerated on the basis of what they personally and individually earn. They may
share expenses, but they do not share income.
89. By way of analogy I note that Section 4.2.1 of Part II of the IBA Guidelines includes on that Part’s Green
List of matters that do not require to be disclosed that: “A firm, in association or in alliance with the
arbitrator’s law firm, but that does not share significant fees or other revenues with the arbitrator’s
law firm, renders services to one of the parties, or an affiliate of one of the parties, in an unrelated
matter” (emphasis added). This underlines the significance of fee-sharing for the purposes of
disclosure obligations.
90. Another crucial difference in this context is that members of chambers have no right to be provided
with details of each other’s professional activities. The implications of this on the disclosure
requirements placed on an arbitrator member of chambers are apparent. It would be unworkable,
indeed futile, to seek to impose an obligation to disclose details of instructions received by other
members of chambers, when the arbitrator has no access to, and no right to demand access to, that
information. Even if a member of chambers has somehow learned of the existence of certain
instructions being given to members of chambers (for example through media reports), to impose a
general obligation of disclosure regarding instructions to other members of chambers would be
unworkable.
91. The fact that there are these important distinguishing features between chambers and law firms is
reflected in the IBA Guidelines, which include the statement in the Explanation to General Standard 6
of the IBA Guidelines that:

"Although barristers' chambers should not be equated with law firms for the purpose of conflicts and
no general standard is proffered for barristers' chambers, disclosure may be warranted in view of the
relationship among barristers, parties or counsel."
92. Against that background how is the position of a potential arbitrator who is a member of a set of
chambers to be assessed? In the context of modern international arbitration, the notion that the
arbitrator can ignore as completely irrelevant the fact that he or she is a member of chambers is
unsustainable. As the IBA Guidelines explain, disclosure may be warranted in view of the relationships
among members of chambers.17 But equally, as reflected in the IBA Guidelines, it would be quite
wrong to assimilate chambers with a law firm and I reject any suggestion that I should do so.
93. The fair-minded observer knowledgeable of the facts and circumstances would consider the nature of
the relationship between the arbitrator and the other members of chambers. He or she would be
aware of the characteristics of membership of chambers described above. In those circumstances, I
reject the suggestion that an informed third-party would conclude that there were justifiable doubts
regarding the impartiality or independence of an arbitrator solely on the basis of instructions received
or to be received from a particular party on other matters by other members of the arbitrator’s
chambers. That is particularly so in a case such as this where the contribution to the overall chambers’
workload of instructions by the party appearing in the arbitration is extremely limited.
94. Accordingly, I find that an informed third party would not consider the volume and frequency of
instructions given to the relevant [X Chambers’] Members to be such as to give rise to an appearance
of bias on the part of [A].

108. The Claimant maintains that it “was and is entitled to receive explanations to address its concerns”
and refers to what it describes as the “occlusive tone” adopted regarding the relationship of [A] and

Decision 7 - 24

109. Whilst [A] was forthcoming with answers to several of the questions asked, particularly with regard to
his prior appointments, it is clear that in a number of instances, notably questions (f) to (k), [A]
effectively declined to give a substantive answer to the questions raised. The Claimant indicates that
certain questions, notably the financial terms of [A]’s appointment in the Arbitration, were not
answered as fully as it would have wished. Be that as it may, the questions were answered and no
specific follow-up requests for information were made prior to the bringing of the Challenge.
110. There were two bases on which [A] has effectively declined to give a substantive answer to the
questions raised. One was that he had already disclosed relevant matters and the other was that the
questions relate to the internal business practices of [X Chambers] or its members, the relevance of
or entitlement to which was disputed. [A] also relied in this regard on the fact that members of
chambers have no right to know what other members of chambers are working on.
111. I find that a number of the questions posed to [A] were very broad and went beyond that which was
relevant or necessary to satisfy the concerns that had been raised by the Claimant. Others were not
questions that he would be in a position to answer because they relate to the affairs of other members
of chambers. This would apply, for example, to questions about whether [A] had “ever” shared clerking
or secretarial services with the relevant [X Chambers’] Members and what the financing arrangements
were on matters in which the relevant [X Chambers’] Members were instructed. This seems to me a
relevant consideration when assessing [A]’s responses overall and his alleged failure to answer the
Claimant’s questions.
112. The question before me is whether the way in which [A] dealt with the questions posed to him gives
rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence. For the reasons set out in paragraph
75 above, I find that in all the circumstances it does not. I find that a fair-minded and informed
observer would consider it reasonable that if [A] felt he had no further disclosures to make, or that he
was being asked for information that it was not appropriate for him to give, he was entitled to say so.
Again the issue here is not whether his answers were objectively right or wrong, but whether, taken
as a whole, in answering as he did [A]’s conduct gave rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or
independence. I find that it did not.
The Claimant’s Concerns Taken as a Whole
113. I have rejected the Challenge on the basis of each of the concerns raised by the Claimant. I must also
consider whether those matters would, on a cumulative basis, provide grounds for justifiable doubts
as to [A]’s impartiality or independence.
114. In paragraph 62 et seq. of the Challenge the Claimant asserts that the totality of the circumstances
warrants [A]’s disqualification. The Claimant relies cumulatively on the facts and circumstances set
out in paragraph 29 above and says that they are similar to those that justified disqualification in the
Slovenia case.
115. The Claimant lays particular emphasis on three factors arising in Slovenia which it says are similar to
the present case. The first of these is that the perception of bias must be judged against the
expectations and characteristics of the specific parties. I have addressed this above and find that the
test to be applied is an objective one. The second factor is described as “the Respondent’s insistent
refusal of disclosure…[of] the nature of the interaction” and the third was the alleged lateness of the
disclosure about the circumstances giving rise to concern.
Decision 7 - 25

116. The Respondent emphasises that the Slovenia case is seen as controversial and in any event the
tribunal in Slovenia made clear that they were not laying down any hard-and-fast rule to the effect
that barristers from the same chambers are always precluded from being involved as arbitrator and
counsel in the same case. Rather it depends on all relevant circumstances. In any event the
Respondent says that under English law the fact that an arbitrator and counsel are from the same
chambers would never, of itself, give rise to apparent bias.
117. In my view both Slovenia and a number of the English law authorities to which the Parties referred19
were dealing with a different situation from that which is before me. In Slovenia objection was taken
to the introduction at a late stage in the case of counsel from a set of chambers of which the President
of the tribunal was a door-tenant. In other words the concern related to the relationship between
members of the same chambers both of whom were participating, in different roles, in the same
arbitration (the “relationship scenario”). The issues to which the relationship scenario gives rise may
provide some general assistance as to the position of arbitrators who are members of barristers’
chambers, but they are not the same as those in the present case. Here the concerns relate to prior
appointments, information barriers between different cases and the impact (if any) of the volume of
work a set of chambers receives from a party to an arbitration (or its affiliates) where a member of
chambers is sitting as arbitrator.
118. Even focussing upon the second and third factors identified by the Claimant relating to disclosure, I
find that the Slovenia case is of no real assistance. In that case the issues concerning disclosure arose
in the context of the relationship scenario and related to a refusal to disclose what the counsel’s role
was to be at a forthcoming hearing and the late stage in the proceedings at which his involvement was
disclosed.
119. The question of disclosure in a Slovenia type of situation is addressed in part in paragraph 3.3.2 of the
Orange List in Part II of the IBA Guidelines. That paragraph specifically contemplates disclosure where:
“The arbitrator and another arbitrator, or the counsel for one of the parties, are members of the same
barristers’ chambers.” This provision was highlighted in [C]’s 17 September letter referred to in
paragraph 16 above. It is not, however, apposite here as none of the relevant [X Chambers’] Members
are involved as counsel in the Arbitration. Similarly, the Claimant’s submission that [D]’s insistence
that the presiding arbitrator in the Arbitration should not be from the same chambers as either of the
two existing arbitrators does not seem to me to have any bearing on the issues before me, and I do
not find it either “remarkable” or a “double-standard”.
120. Nor do I find Halliburton Company v Chubb Bermuda Insurance Ltd [2018] EWCA Civ 817, relied upon
by the Claimant, to be of assistance in the present circumstances. That case involved the failure by an
arbitrator to disclose his involvement in other arbitrations which the court found he should have
disclosed. That is not the case here and there is no suggestion that [A] is involved in any other cases,
as counsel or arbitrator, that he should have, but has not, disclosed to the Parties.
121. In this case, [A] has disclosed certain prior appointments none of which, alone or cumulatively, provide
grounds for justifiable doubts as to his impartiality or independence. The disclosure in relation to one
of those prior appointments was made 15 days after [A]’s appointment which was a short and

Decision 7 - 26

inconsequential delay as regards the conduct of the Arbitration. The other complaints regarding the
volume and frequency of instructions of the relevant [X Chambers’] Members, including by
[Government B], and [A]’s provision of information regarding information barriers and the 14
questions raised by the Claimant, do not give rise to justifiable doubts as to [A]’s impartiality or
independence. In all the circumstances I find that, even considered on a cumulative basis, the concerns
raised by the Claimant do not provide grounds for his disqualification or removal as arbitrator in the
Arbitration.
Decision
122. For the reasons stated I CONCLUDE AND DECIDE that the Claimant has not shown justifiable doubts
as to [A]’s impartiality or independence, and the Challenge is dismissed.
123. I further DECLARE that all costs incurred in connection with the Challenge are reserved to the decision
of the Tribunal in due course in accordance with Articles 38 to 40 of the 1976 UNCITRAL Rules.
